translations.idiomatic: Pian made Zhang Shouyi and Yongzhi commissioners of the Left and Right Moye armies, with a full general-staff complement of officers. Their weapons were the finest; their dress was sumptuous. Each time they went out, nearly a thousand attendants escorted them.

sentences.zh: 用之侍妾百餘人，自奉奢靡，用度不足，輒留三司綱輸其家。

translations.literal: Yongzhi kept over a hundred concubines and lived in lavish self-indulgence; when expenses fell short he would detain the Sancsi tax convoys and divert them to his household.
translations.idiomatic: Yongzhi kept more than a hundred concubines and lived in extravagant luxury. When funds ran short he simply diverted the Sancsi tax convoys to his own household.

sentences.zh: 用之猶慮人洩其奸謀，乃言於駢曰：「神仙不難致，但恨學道者不能絕俗累，故不肯降臨耳！

translations.literal: Yongzhi still feared men would leak his treacherous designs; he therefore said to Pian, "Immortals are not hard to summon; only one regrets that seekers of the Way cannot sever worldly burdens, and so they are unwilling to descend!"
translations.idiomatic: Still fearing exposure of his schemes, Yongzhi told Pian, "Immortals are easy to summon—if only seekers of the Way could cast off worldly attachments. That is why they will not come down!"

sentences.zh: 」駢乃悉去姬妾，謝絕人事，賓客、將吏皆不得見。

translations.literal: Pian then dismissed all his concubines, broke off human contact, and guests and generals alike were denied audience.
translations.idiomatic: Pian then dismissed all his concubines, shut himself off from the world, and refused audience to guests and officers alike.

sentences.zh: 有不得已見之者，皆先令沐浴繼祓，然後見，拜起才畢，已復引出。

translations.literal: Those who had to be received were first made to bathe and undergo purification rites, then received; scarcely had bows and greetings ended when they were led out again.
translations.idiomatic: Anyone who had to be received was first made to bathe and undergo purification rites; the moment formal greetings were done, he was ushered out again.

sentences.zh: 由是用之得專行威福，無所忌憚，境內不復知有駢矣。

translations.literal: Thus Yongzhi came to wield authority and favor without restraint, without fear; within the borders none anymore knew there was a Pian.
translations.idiomatic: From then on Yongzhi wielded absolute power without restraint. Within the circuit, no one any longer knew there was a Gao Pian.

sentences.zh: 王鐸將兩川、興元之軍屯靈感寺，涇原屯京西，易定、河中屯渭北，邠寧、鳳翔屯興平，保大、定難屯渭橋，忠武屯武功，官軍四集。

translations.literal: Wang Duo led the armies of the Two Chuan and Xingyuan to encamp at Linggan Temple; Jingyuan at Jingxi; Yiding and Hezhong at north of the Wei; Binning and Fengxiang at Xingping; Baoda and Dingnan at Wei Bridge; Zhongwu at Wugong—government troops gathered on four sides.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Duo led the armies of the Two Chuan and Xingyuan to camp at Linggan Temple; Jingyuan at Jingxi; Yiding and Hezhong north of the Wei; Binning and Fengxiang at Xingping; Baoda and Dingnan at Wei Bridge; Zhongwu at Wugong—imperial armies converged from every side.

sentences.zh: 黃巢勢已蹙，號令所行不出同、華。

translations.literal: Huang Chao's strength was already cramped; orders he issued reached no farther than Tong and Hua.
translations.idiomatic: Huang Chao's position was already desperate; his orders no longer reached beyond Tong and Hua.

sentences.zh: 民避亂皆入深山築柵自保，農事俱廢，長安城中斗米直三十緡。

translations.literal: The people, fleeing disorder, all entered deep mountains and built palisades to protect themselves; farming was entirely abandoned; in Chang'an city a dou of rice fetched thirty strings of cash.
translations.idiomatic: Civilians fleeing the chaos retreated into the mountains and built palisades for protection. Farming ceased entirely. In Chang'an, a dou of rice sold for thirty strings of cash.

sentences.zh: 賊賣人於官軍以為糧，官軍或執山柵之民鬻之，人直數百緡，以肥瘠論價。

translations.literal: The rebels sold people to the government army for grain; the government army sometimes seized people from mountain palisades and sold them; a human fetched several hundred strings of cash, priced by plumpness or leanness.
translations.idiomatic: The rebels sold captives to the imperial army for grain. Imperial troops sometimes rounded up people from the mountain palisades and sold them in turn—several hundred strings of cash per person, priced by fat or thin.
